headline: Genri is 原 (gen, “principle”) plus 理 (ri, “theory”).
Furi was puri in Old Japanese, the continuative stem of 振る (furu, “to swing”).
Kyōka is 強 (kyō, “strengthen”) plus 化 (ka, “cause to become”).
Ku, “trouble”, is from Middle Chinese 苦 (MC khuX, “suffering”).
Kureru is related to 黒 (kuro, “black”).
Junban is 順 (jun, “order”) plus 番 (ban, “numerical order”).
Suki was originally the continuative stem of 透く (suku, “to leave a gap”).
Aji went from adi through adzi to azi, from Proto-Japonic *anti.
Shita is from Old Japanese, from Proto-Japonic *sita.
Ba, “place”, is an alteration of Old Japanese 庭 (nipa), modern 庭 (niwa, “garden, yard”).
Gichō is 議 (“discussion”) plus 長 (“head”).
Make is the continuative stem of 負ける (makeru, “to lose, to be defeated”).
Zonzuru is 存 (zon) plus する, with suru voiced to zuru.
Kaeru, “to interchange”, is from Old Japanese かふ (kapu), in the lower bigrade pattern.
Ōsama is 王 (ō) plus 様 (-sama).
Itami is a nominalization of 痛む (itamu, “to cause pain, hurt”).
Iyagaru is 嫌 (iya, “despised”) plus がる (-garu, “to act like”).
Sei, “sex, gender”, is from Middle Chinese 性 (MC sjengH, “nature of something, inherent quality”), the kan'on, so a later borrowing.
Daimeishi is 代 (dai, “replacement”) plus 名詞 (meishi, “noun”), as it stands in for a noun.
Kawaigaru is 可愛い (kawaii, “cute, adorable”) plus がる (-garu, “feeling or thinking that way”).
Kin'niku is 筋 (“muscle; tendon”) plus 肉 (“flesh”).
Kūsō is Middle Chinese 空想, literally “fictional, fabricated + think, thought”; the fantasy sense is first cited in Japanese to 1886.
Dakara is だ (“to be”) plus から (“because”).
Nobasu, “to extend”, is cognate with 伸ばす (nobasu, “to grow, to spread”).
Heibon is Middle Chinese 平凡, literally “even, flat + in every case”.
Shinkū is first attested in the Kaifūsō anthology of 751, and its modern sense of vacuum in 1876.
Kumi is the continuative stem of 組む (kumu, “to assemble”).
In chinō, 知 is a daiyōji replacing 智.
Obi is the continuative stem of 帯ぶ (obu, “to put something on the body”), first attested in the Nihon Shoki of 720 CE.
Kōun is probably from Middle Chinese 幸運, literally “lucky fortune”.
